Introduction to the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel Model

dnsr package

2026-10-09

Source: vignettes/dns-model-introduction.Rmd
dns-model-introduction.Rmd

Overview

The dnsr package implements the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel (DNS) model for yield curve modelling. This vignette walks the whole workflow: fitting the curve, estimating how its factors move, simulating forward, and pricing off the result.

Everything here runs against treasury_yields, a six-year panel of real U.S. Treasury curves that ships with the package, so none of it needs a FRED API key. For live data see vignette("fred-api-setup", package = "dnsr"), and for the YUIMA simulation engine see vignette("dnsr-yuima-integration", package = "dnsr").

library(dnsr)
data(treasury_yields)

dim(treasury_yields)
#> [1] 1501   12
range(treasury_yields$Date)
#> [1] "2019-01-02" "2024-12-31"

The frame is the shape every function in the package expects: a Date column followed by one column per maturity, named by maturity in years, with yields in decimal form.

treasury_yields[1:3, 1:6]
#>         Date 0.0833   0.25    0.5      1      2
#> 1 2019-01-02 0.0240 0.0242 0.0251 0.0260 0.0250
#> 2 2019-01-03 0.0242 0.0241 0.0247 0.0250 0.0239
#> 3 2019-01-04 0.0240 0.0242 0.0251 0.0257 0.0250

The Nelson-Siegel Model

The Nelson-Siegel model is a parsimonious parametric model for the yield curve. It expresses the yield at each maturity through three factors:

y(m)=β1+β2(1−e−λmλm)+β3(1−e−λmλm−e−λm)y(m) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m}\right) + \beta_3 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m} - e^{-\lambda m}\right)

where

  • y(m)y(m) is the yield at maturity mm,
  • β1\beta_1 is the long-term level of interest rates,
  • β2\beta_2 is the slope, short-term minus long-term,
  • β3\beta_3 is the curvature, the size of the hump,
  • λ\lambda controls how fast the factor loadings decay.

The loadings are what give each factor its interpretation: the level loads equally on every maturity, the slope loads most at the short end and decays to zero, and the curvature peaks in the middle of the curve.

plot_dns_loadings(lambda = 0.0609)

Raising λ\lambda pulls the curvature hump toward shorter maturities:

plot_dns_loadings(lambda = 0.4)

Dynamic Extension

The DNS model lets the three factors vary over time, each as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process:

dβi(t)=κi(θi−βi(t))dt+σidWi(t)d\beta_i(t) = \kappa_i(\theta_i - \beta_i(t))dt + \sigma_i dW_i(t)

with κi\kappa_i the speed of mean reversion, θi\theta_i the long-run mean, σi\sigma_i the volatility and Wi(t)W_i(t) a Wiener process. Fitting the curve is therefore two steps: a cross-sectional fit on each date, then a time-series estimate of how the resulting factors move.

Fitting a Single Curve

fit_ns_model() fits one cross-section. The "profile" method solves the three betas in closed form at each λ\lambda and searches only over λ\lambda, so it needs no starting values:

maturities <- as.numeric(setdiff(names(treasury_yields), "Date"))
latest <- as.numeric(treasury_yields[nrow(treasury_yields), -1])

curve <- fit_ns_model(maturities, latest, method = "profile")
#> Warning in fit_ns_model(maturities, latest, method = "profile"): Nelson-Siegel
#> fit rests on a parameter bound (lambda); the factor decomposition is not
#> identified. Widen lower_bounds/upper_bounds or check the yield scale.
curve
#> Nelson-Siegel curve fit
#>   beta1 (level)     0.04988
#>   beta2 (slope)     -0.00617
#>   beta3 (curvature) -0.01404
#>   lambda            0.50000
#>   rmse              4.95 bp over 11 maturities
#>   at bound          lambda (decomposition not identified)

That warning is worth taking seriously rather than silencing. The fit reports any parameter that came to rest on one of its bounds, because a clamped fit can still look respectable on RMSE while the factor decomposition means nothing, and L-BFGS-B reports convergence at a bound, so success alone cannot tell you.

curve$at_bound
#>  beta1  beta2  beta3 lambda 
#>  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE

Here the default ceiling on λ\lambda, 0.5, is genuinely binding: this curve wants a faster decay than the conventional value allows. Given room, it finds an interior optimum and fits better:

wider <- fit_ns_model(maturities, latest, method = "profile",
                      lower_bounds = c(-1, -1, -1, 0.01),
                      upper_bounds = c(1, 1, 1, 5))
c(lambda = wider$parameters[["lambda"]], rmse_bp = wider$rmse * 10000)
#>    lambda   rmse_bp 
#> 0.6687707 4.4314318

Fitting the Panel

fit_dns_model() fits every date. The window is selected by date, so it does not matter which row order the panel arrives in.

For a panel there is a choice to make that does not arise for a single curve. If λ\lambda is estimated freely it varies from date to date – on this data from 0.04 to 0.50 – and then β2\beta_2 on one date does not mean the same thing as β2\beta_2 on the next, because the loading it multiplies has changed shape. The betas stop being a comparable time series, which is precisely what the next step needs them to be.

Standard DNS practice, following Diebold and Li, therefore fixes λ\lambda at a single value for the whole panel. It costs cross-sectional fit – about 14 basis points median here against 7 with λ\lambda free – and buys factors that can be modelled over time:

recent <- fit_dns_model(treasury_yields, n_days = 250, show_progress = FALSE,
                        lambda_constraint = "fixed", initial_lambda = 0.0609)
recent
#> Dynamic Nelson-Siegel fit
#>   250 curves, 2024-01-02 to 2024-12-31
#>   maturities         0.0833  0.2500  0.5000  1.0000  2.0000  3.0000  5.0000  7.0000 10.0000 20.0000 30.0000
#>   rmse              23.01 bp median, 42.01 bp worst
#>   lambda            0.0609 median
#>   success rate      100.0%

summary() gives the distribution of each factor and of the fit error:

summary(recent)
#> Dynamic Nelson-Siegel fit
#>   250 curves, 2024-01-02 to 2024-12-31, 100.0% fitted
#> 
#> Factors:
#>             min     mean      max      sd
#> beta1   0.04832  0.10658  0.14015 0.02229
#> beta2  -0.09104 -0.05679 -0.00534 0.02056
#> beta3  -0.18200 -0.11474  0.00968 0.04603
#> lambda  0.06090  0.06090  0.06090 0.00000
#> 
#> Fit error (basis points):
#>    0%   50%   95%  100% 
#>  5.71 23.01 39.97 42.01

Fitted curves against the observations:

plot_yield_curves(treasury_yields, recent, max_plots = 4)

And the factors over time:

factor_plots <- plot_factor_time_series(recent)
factor_plots$factors

factor_plots$rmse

Estimating Factor Dynamics

estimate_dns_dynamics() regresses each factor’s change on its lagged level. By default it samples the factor series at month-ends and estimates at Δt=1/12\Delta t = 1/12: daily cross-sectional refits carry measurement noise that is serially uncorrelated, and an OU regression on daily changes reads that noise as mean reversion, inflating κ\kappa by an order of magnitude.

Because the estimation uses month-ends anyway, fitting only those is enough and is far quicker. warm_start = FALSE makes each cross-section independent of which other dates are in the panel, so these fits are the ones fitting every day would have produced:

month_ends <- treasury_yields[
  !duplicated(format(treasury_yields$Date, "%Y-%m"), fromLast = TRUE),
]
monthly_fit <- fit_dns_model(month_ends, n_days = nrow(month_ends),
                             show_progress = FALSE, warm_start = FALSE,
                             lambda_constraint = "fixed",
                             initial_lambda = 0.0609)

dynamics <- estimate_dns_dynamics(monthly_fit$parameters)
dynamics
#> DNS factor dynamics
#>   estimated on     2019-02-28 to 2024-12-31
#>   sampling         monthly (dt = 1/12), 71 observations
#>   structure        diagonal
#> 
#>                 kappa se_kappa   theta  sigma half_life_y
#> level (b1)     0.6667   0.4748  0.0492 0.0620      1.0397
#> slope (b2)     1.2032   0.6338 -0.0215 0.0594      0.5761
#> curvature (b3) 0.8292   0.5299 -0.0181 0.1243      0.8360
#> 
#>   stable           TRUE (eigenvalues 1.203 0.829 0.667)

The standard errors are worth reading before anything is built on κ\kappa. Mean reversion is weakly identified in a sample this short, and the half-life interval says so:

dynamics$beta1$se
#>      kappa      theta      sigma 
#> 0.47482691 0.03849805 0.00527441
dynamics$beta1$t_value
#>    kappa    theta 
#> 1.404094 1.276968
dynamics$beta1$half_life_ci
#>    lower    upper 
#> 0.433937      Inf

κ\kappa also carries a well-known upward small-sample bias of order 5/T5/T in a sample of TT years, which these standard errors describe nothing about: they are sampling noise, not bias.

Factor innovations are correlated, and the simulation uses that:

round(dynamics$correlation, 3)
#>        beta1  beta2  beta3
#> beta1  1.000 -0.980 -0.986
#> beta2 -0.980  1.000  0.974
#> beta3 -0.986  0.974  1.000

A full mean-reversion matrix

By default the three factors revert independently. structure = "full" estimates the Diebold-Li VAR(1) instead, in which a shock to one factor pulls the others:

full <- estimate_dns_dynamics(monthly_fit$parameters, structure = "full")
round(full$kappa_matrix, 3)
#>        beta1  beta2  beta3
#> beta1 -2.615 -6.952  0.802
#> beta2  2.334  5.767 -0.623
#> beta3  7.148 12.107  0.141

The eigenvalues of that matrix decide whether the system is stable, which a diagonal reconstruction would get wrong whenever the cross terms matter:

round(Re(full$eigenvalues), 3)
#> [1] 1.401 1.401 0.490
full$system_stability
#> [1] TRUE

Simulating Future Yield Curves

The factor system is a linear SDE whose diffusion does not depend on the state, so its transition law over any step is a known Gaussian. engine = "exact" samples that law directly: no discretisation error at any step size, and no extra package.

latest_row <- monthly_fit$parameters[which.max(monthly_fit$parameters$Date), ]
initial_factors <- as.numeric(latest_row[c("beta1", "beta2", "beta3")])

sim_params <- dns_dynamics_to_sim_params(dynamics, lambda = latest_row$lambda)

simulation <- simulate_dns_yield_curves(
  params = sim_params,
  initial_factors = initial_factors,
  maturities = maturities,
  time_horizon = 5,
  n_steps = 60,
  n_paths = 500,
  engine = "exact",
  seed = 1
)
simulation
#> DNS simulation
#>   500 paths, 60 steps over 5 years
#>   engine           exact
#>   terminal factors 0.0482  -0.0203  -0.0152
#>     (sd)           0.0558  0.0402  0.1008
#>   maturities        0.0833  0.2500  0.5000  1.0000  2.0000  3.0000  5.0000  7.0000 10.0000 20.0000 30.0000
#>   terminal yields  2.79  2.79  2.80  2.81  2.82  2.84  2.88  2.92  2.99  3.22  3.43 (% mean)

Simulated curves at a few horizons. The facets follow the calendar rather than sorting lexically, so “Year 5” comes after “Year 3”:

yield_plots <- plot_simulated_yields(
  simulation,
  time_points = c(0, 1, 3, 5),
  path_subset = 1:5
)
yield_plots$yield_curves

The factor paths, as a fan of quantiles across all 500 of them:

plot_simulated_factors(simulation)$level

The YUIMA engine remains available and is the default, for the estimation machinery that comes with it. See vignette("dnsr-yuima-integration", package = "dnsr").

Pricing off a Fitted Curve

A fitted curve is only useful if it discounts cashflows. The DNS curve gives continuously compounded zero rates, so the discount factor at maturity mm is P(m)=exp⁡(−y(m)m)P(m) = \exp(-y(m)\,m):

factors <- matrix(curve$parameters[1:3], nrow = 1)
lambda <- curve$parameters[["lambda"]]

coupon_maturities <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 30)
data.frame(
  maturity = coupon_maturities,
  zero_pct = round(calculate_dns_yields(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ] * 100, 3),
  discount = round(dns_discount_factors(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ], 4),
  price_100 = round(dns_zero_prices(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ], 2),
  par_pct = round(dns_par_yields(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ] * 100, 3)
)
#>   maturity zero_pct discount price_100 par_pct
#> 1      0.5    4.293   0.9788     97.88   4.339
#> 2      1.0    4.249   0.9584     95.84   4.295
#> 3      2.0    4.227   0.9189     91.89   4.272
#> 4      5.0    4.361   0.8041     80.41   4.400
#> 5     10.0    4.596   0.6316     63.16   4.614
#> 6     30.0    4.853   0.2332     23.32   4.827

Par yields are the coupon rate that prices a bullet bond at par. They differ from the zero yields for two reasons that can pull in opposite directions: a compounding convention term, since the curve is continuously compounded while the par rate pays twice a year, and a shape term, since coupons are discounted at the earlier rates rather than the terminal one. The first dominates at the short end and the second further out.

Forward rates come off the same factors:

rbind(
  spot = round(calculate_dns_yields(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ] * 100, 3),
  forward = round(calculate_dns_forwards(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ] * 100, 3)
)
#>          [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]  [,5]  [,6]
#> spot    4.293 4.249 4.227 4.361 4.596 4.853
#> forward 4.234 4.188 4.244 4.649 4.936 4.988

Looking at the Panel

A heatmap of the whole panel shows the 2020 collapse to near-zero short rates and the 2022-2023 inversion:

plot_yield_heatmap(treasury_yields)

Principal components of the daily changes. Decomposing the covariance matrix rather than standardising each maturity first is the usual convention for yield curves, and is what produces the familiar level, slope and curvature shapes:

pca <- plot_yield_pca(treasury_yields, scale = FALSE)
round(pca$var_explained[1:3], 4)
#> [1] 0.7160 0.1087 0.0991
pca$plots$weights

The first three components are the empirical counterpart of the model’s three factors, which is the reason a three-factor curve works as well as it does.

Comparing Term Structure Models

compare_term_structure_models() fits several curves to one cross-section and reports the error of each, in basis points:

comparison <- compare_term_structure_models(
  treasury_yields,
  models = c("NS", "NSS", "Spline")
)
comparison$metrics
#>                    Model     RMSE      MAE  MaxError
#> 1          Nelson-Siegel 8.873355 7.506098 15.404612
#> 2 Nelson-Siegel-Svensson 3.542643 2.502529  8.621915
#> 3           Cubic Spline 5.561295 3.995767 11.985578
comparison$plot

Nelson-Siegel-Svensson adds a second curvature term with its own decay, so it nests Nelson-Siegel and must fit at least as well; the question is whether the two extra parameters are worth it. A smoothing spline will generally beat both on in-sample error while saying nothing about the shape, which is the trade the parametric models exist to make.
